title: NASA’s Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth
excerpt: Voyager 1, depicted in this artist’s concept, reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18. Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday. “Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.” Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space. Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum. A ray of sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1. For comparison, a light-year is 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers). Even though the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, the spacecraft is sending what is called a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth. Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone. They continue to analyze the issue impacting the science and engineering data. Humanity’s only probes in interstellar space, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Managed by JPL, they were only the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery, transforming our understanding of these worlds and their moons. Voyager 2 went on to study the ethereal ice giants, Neptune and Uranus. Both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances. “Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.” In addition to their suite of scientific instruments , the Voyager probes carry a Golden Record , a gold-plated copper phonograph compiling images and sounds from Earth, as a message to any advanced civilization that might one day find it. “Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. “Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.” Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, transformed our understanding of the solar system through their exploration of the outer planets. In 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made spacecraft to enter interstellar space. On Nov. 18, 2026, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. Milestones, challenges Traveling about 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), Voyager 1 in 2012 became the first spacecraft to leave the heliosphere , the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the Sun that deflects cosmic radiation, and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2, taking a different trajectory, crossed the boundary in 2018. “The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. “One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.” Creative engineering solutions have enabled the probes to conserve energy and overcome challenges related to aging hardware, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer on the spacecraft. Earlier this year, engineers successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives — a move not without risk — to help the spacecraft make the most of its 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator . Essentially a nuclear battery, the generator converts heat from decaying plutonium into electricity. With the plutonium supply continually depleting, both Voyager probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. The latest energy-saving effort is expected to provide enough power for both spacecraft to keep their current suite of science instruments operating until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer. As with all NASA spacecraft that venture to and beyond the Moon, communication between Earth and the Voyager probes is managed by the agency’s Deep Space Network , large antennas located at three facilities around the world. “We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. “Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars.” For more information about NASA’s Voyager mission, visit: https://science.nasa.gov/mission/voyager/ -end- Abbey Interrante / Karen Fox Headquarters, Washington 202-358-1600 abbey.a.interrante@nasa.gov / karen.c.fox@nasa.gov Calla Cofield Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, Calif. 626-808-2469 calla.e.cofield@jpl.nasa.gov Share Details Last Updated Nov 19, 2026 Editor Jessica Taveau Location NASA Headquarters Related Terms Voyager 1 Heliophysics Heliophysics Division Jet Propulsion Laboratory Science Mission Directorate The Solar System The Sun

Golestan is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the great surviving monuments of Iran’s Qajar dynasty, which ruled from 1789 until 1925. Within hours of the strike, UNESCO reported the damage and noted that cultural property is protected under international law during armed conflict. The palace was not only an early casualty of the U.S.-Iran war, but a symbolically potent one, too. And as my colleague Mehrnoush Soroush at the Center for Ancient Middle Eastern Landscapes has documented , Golestan is not alone. Since the war in Iran began in February 2026, reports of damage to heritage sites have poured in from all across Iran. I know that damaged buildings — no matter how valuable — cannot compare with the human costs of war. But the images from Golestan have particular resonance to me, an archaeologist who studies the history of relations between Iran and the United States . It also cuts against a history of cooperation between American and Iranian archaeologists, in which Americans worked to preserve, rather than destroy, Iranian heritage. Digging in, together I have spent years researching how archaeologists, museums and cultural officials from the two countries worked together before the Iranian Revolution of 1979 . My earlier research has examined how archaeology became entangled with American foreign aid and Iranian development programs during the 1960s, and I am currently writing a book on the history of U.S.-Iranian heritage diplomacy over the past century. I believe that history offers another way of thinking about what has been lost in the current conflict. Long before Iran and the U.S. became adversaries, cultural heritage provided a setting in which people from the two countries learned how to work together. American archaeologists began excavating in Iran in the early 1930s . In those days, the relationship was unequal: American museums sought access to archaeological sites and, under agreements with the Iranian government, received portions of the objects they excavated under the colonial system of partage . As a result, museums across the U.S. still hold substantial collections of Iranian antiquities. The site of an archeological dig at Hasanlu, Iran. Wikimedia Commons , CC BY The terms of the relationship changed considerably during the 1960s, as the U.S. and Iran intensified their connections. At the same time that thousands of American professionals, educators, businesspeople, scholars and others came to work and live in Iran, the country revised its antiquities laws and expanded its own archaeological institutions, universities and museums , resulting in, among other things, a major tourism boom . American archaeologists still wanted permission to dig at Iranian sites, but they increasingly operated within a system controlled by Iranian officials. In return, American institutions contributed funding and access to laboratories, specialist knowledge, graduate education and connections to an international scholarly community. American archaeological projects in Iran drew on large networks of such connections. Scholars working on the Deh Luran Plain in southwestern Iran, for example, depended on Iranian government agencies, the U.S. Embassy, American universities and museums, development organizations and scientific laboratories. Botanical remains, animal bones and other materials moved through specialist laboratories abroad, while Iranian officials worked alongside foreign researchers in the field. Collaboration under the shah By the 1970s, fieldwork projects were increasingly becoming joint enterprises, based on formal partnerships between institutions and cooperative leadership. Iranian archaeological authorities employed American specialists to help survey areas threatened by dams and other development projects , while Iranian archaeologists increasingly took leading roles in the field. Meanwhile, students moved in greater numbers between Tehran, Chicago, Philadelphia and New York. Museums organized traveling exhibitions , and Iran hosted international scholarly congresses devoted to its history and archaeology. It can’t be ignored that these collaborations flourished during a period when Iran, under Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi, was a close American ally . While the terms of the relationship increasingly favored Iran, they were still marked by geopolitical inequalities. American universities and museums possessed resources that Iranian institutions often lacked – not only financially and in terms of human capital, but physically, in the form of collections of artifacts that had previously been taken out of Iran. Yet the collaborations also developed lives of their own, as American scholars returned year after year. The archeological site at Persepolis, Iran, in 1976. Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA Post-revolutionary changes The Islamic Revolution exposed both how extensive and fragile this network was. Even as the crisis that began in 1978 deepened, American archaeologists did not initially assume that their Iranian partnerships were finished. At Malyan, the remains of ancient Anshan, archaeologist William Sumner proposed continuing to pay a watchman to protect the site, while maintaining contact with Iranian colleagues so research could eventually resume. That did not come to pass. And much of the American-Iranian archaeological enterprise collapsed as diplomatic relations between the two countries soured after the Islamic Republic took 52 American diplomats and civilians hostage in 1979 and Washington sided with Baghdad during the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s. But the example of the 1960s and ‘70s points toward a sometimes less visible part of diplomacy: relationships accumulated through repeated practical work. International relations expert Trita Parsi makes this point in his history of the negotiations that produced the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement . In “ Losing an Enemy ,” based on interviews with participants on both sides, Parsi describes the working relationship that developed between U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif. This is not to say that their personal rapport produced the nuclear agreement by itself. Naturally, presidents had to authorize negotiations, diplomats at all levels had to find compromises, and both governments had to conclude that an agreement served their interests. But contemporary reporting described that relationship as one built on professional respect and repeated close proximity. In other words, Kerry and Zarif spent enough time negotiating together to understand each other’s constraints and establish a working relationship despite the hostility between their two governments. That kind of personal working relationship can assist diplomacy – not just at the highest levels but more broadly across civil society. Sports diplomacy has long been acknowledged; so too the sharing of zoological “gifts.” My research shows that archaeology has long had an important a place in these kinds of cultural exchanges as well. Iranians gather on April 4, 2026, to protest strikes on Iran’s historic sites. Atta Kenare/AFP via Getty Images Today, Iranian conservation specialists are sorting and cataloging shattered fragments from Golestan Palace while attempting to repair damage at heritage sites around the country . At the same time, American and Iranian officials are still looking for ways to end the conflict. I don’t know what U.S.-Iranian relations will look like when the fighting eventually ends, but damaged buildings and monuments will need to be repaired and conserved. If my inbox is anything to go by, Iranian scholars still want to work together with American colleagues. And if a larger political opening for U.S.-Iranian rapprochement ever arrives, the relationships built by those who steward and study Iran’s heritage may matter more than they first appear. title: Nvidia isn’t the first company to dump a misbehaving CEO – history shows it’s in the interest of corporate boards to act
excerpt: Nvidia's board is now coming under more scrutiny for its own oversight after it ousted its CEO, Jensen Huang. Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis. This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the ouster of its CEO , Jensen Huang. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd. Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit. Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Meanwhile, an internal petition allegedly signed by more than 1,600 Nvidia employees has also called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement. As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board made the right call. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something. CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization. But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. If the board is earning billions , it’s even more difficult. The costs of misconduct One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows. One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it. Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well. In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it. In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks . Another issue is moral hazard : when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation. My research has found that risk to be high. When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first. Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991. Former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker attracted much more negative attention after his second DUI arrest compared to his first. CHIP SOMODEVILLA/POOL/AFP via Getty Images Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship. In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future? A question of culture Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake. CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive. Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees. It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct. For now, the public debate has largely centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight. It’s a board’s duty to protect its organization from managers who go astray, as legendary investor Warren Buffett noted : “It isn’t fundamental dishonesty that causes people to go in a different direction. It’s human nature. There are plenty of people who are really decent people, intelligent people. … But they just don’t come to grips with reality. And boards usually don’t push them to.” Michael Nalick does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

title: Eurovision took its song contest to Asia – bringing its political drama and cultural tropes along for the ride
excerpt: Laos' contestant, Thinla, performs at the Eurovision Song Contest Asia 2026 in Bangkok on Nov. 14, 2026. Chanakarn Laosarakham/AFP via Getty Images ABBA and Céline Dion came to the world’s attention thanks to the Eurovision Song Contest, an annual showcase of pop music, camp and spectacle. Filipino singer Carmelle is hoping that the Eurovision Song Contest Asia will serve as a similar springboard to international fame. On Nov. 14, 2026, Carmelle bested entries from 11 Asian countries to be crowned the Asian edition’s first-ever winner . The competition marked Eurovision’s boldest expansion of its format in its 70-year history. As a scholar of contemporary European popular music and politics , I study the ways in which Eurovision shapes notions of what it looks like and sounds like to be European. Knowing that the Asian edition would be organized by European broadcasting executives, I wanted to see how closely Eurovision Asia would resemble the flagship Eurovision, or whether it would carve out an identity of its own. Stops and starts Eurovision’s proposed expansion into Asia dates back to 2008, when the European Broadcasting Union – the transnational coalition of public service media organizations that has organized the Eurovision Song Contest since 1956 – announced plans for “ Our Sound – The Asia-Pacific Song Contest .” Originally slated to debut in 2010, the project never materialized. On March 31, 2026, however, Voxovation, a European-led production company that oversees the development of Eurovision’s spinoffs, announced that Bangkok would host the inaugural Asian competition in partnership with Thailand’s Channel 3 and S2O Productions. Eurovision Asia is now the second European Broadcasting Union-licensed global spinoff to make the airwaves. In 2022, Voxovation organized the American Song Contest , which included original songs by artists from all 50 U.S. states, five territories and Washington. Despite being promoted to the American public in a Super Bowl commercial featuring hosts Kelly Clarkson and Snoop Dogg, the competition failed to attract a large viewership and the spinoff wasn’t renewed. ‘You will be blown away!’ Given two decades of uncertainty, as well as the failure of Voxovation’s U.S. spinoff, some critics doubted whether the Asian version would succeed. And for a moment, it looked like everything might fall apart: In late October 2026, the Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet reported that Eurovision Asia’s original budget of approximately US$4.5 million had been reduced by US$1 million. The European Broadcasting Union, however, confirmed that the show would go on as planned, and at 8:30 p.m. Bangkok time on Nov. 14, the show’s two hosts, Thai media personalities Woody Milintachinda and Cindy Bishop, welcomed viewers from around the world tuning in via television broadcast and the YouTube livestream. “Maybe you’ve never heard of Eurovision before, or maybe you’re one of the hardcore Eurofans,” said Bishop. “It doesn’t matter, because you will be blown away by the talent here tonight!” For the next two-and-a-half hours, each country’s representative performed an original song, with Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên opening the show with her song “Em Tiên” (“Fairy Maiden”). Vietnam’s entry had many of the spectacular ingredients of an ideal Eurovision entry: bilingual lyrics, large props, flashy outfits and a dance break. The song’s instrumentation included a flute accompanying Tiên’s melody and a bamboo xylophone. It concluded with a second, high-energy dance break reminiscent of electronic dance music genres. Vietnam’s live performance at Eurovision Asia 2026. The song’s use of traditional Asian musical signifiers followed the approach of the European entrants that have incorporated folk traditions to promote their national cultures to an international audience. For example, Ukraine’s 2004 winning entry, Ruslana’s “ Wild Dances ,” opened with the trembita , a long alpine horn associated with the Hutsul people of the Carpathian Mountains. Armenia’s 2008 entry, Sirusho’s “ Qele, Qele ,” similarly combined a traditional Armenian duduk flute , zurna trumpet and dhol drums with an upbeat dance track and contemporary pop vocals. While some scholars claim that these musical gestures strategically romanticize and exoticize regional cultures , it’s a way to fuse national identity with modern music. Other Eurovision Asia entrants also pulled from this playbook. Mongolia’s singer, Beck, wore a deel , the country’s traditional robe, while performing . He also incorporated a traditional Mongolian string instrument into his performance. Voting, which was open to the general public via an online form, began just before the first performance. Viewers were allotted eight free votes, on the condition that they had to vote for at least three different countries . They could purchase 10 additional votes. The public accounted for half the votes, while a jury made up of representatives from each nation accounted for the other half. Carmelle’s winning song – a Filipina women’s empowerment anthem titled “Sobra-Sobra” (“Too Much”) – featured a repeated musical line played by a kulintang , a Filipino percussion instrument, and a frenetic dance break. The song’s bridge was rapped in Tagalog , the country’s national language. As part of her reward, Carmelle will perform “Sobra-Sobra” at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Burgas, Bulgaria. The Philippines’ winning live performance at Eurovision Asia 2026. Europe, Asia … the world? No Eurovision competition would be complete without a measure of political controversy. From broadcaster boycotts over Israel’s participation amid the war in Gaza to suspicions that Franco’s Spain rigged the 1968 Eurovision vote in its favor , political disputes have long been part of the competition. Normally, political statements are not permitted in Eurovision , though exceptions have been made for humanitarian causes. Ukraine’s victory in Eurovision 2022 took place just a few months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the former Soviet republic. Oleh Psiuk, the frontman of Ukraine’s entrant, Kalush Orchestra, pleaded for support for Ukraine at the end of the performance, which the European Broadcasting Union ended up allowing. During Eurovision Song Contest Asia, Malaysia found itself at the center of controversy. Malaysian entrant Aina Abdul, who wears a hijab in her public appearances, performed her song “Bluest Sky.” While Abdul was seen as a possible favorite, Malaysian audiences claimed that she ultimately did not score enough points due to Islamophobia . Malaysia’s live performance at Eurovision Asia 2026. Another controversy arose due to the Malaysian broadcaster TV3’s coverage of the show. During the results segment at the end of the show, the camera feed of the Filipino spokesperson, the drag queen Vice Ganda, was cut from the Malaysian broadcast. Malaysian broadcasting laws restrict the airing of drag and LGBTQ+ content on television, radio and digital platforms. In a comment to The Guardian , Eurovision Director Martin Green said, “We are surprised and disappointed to learn that the broadcast of Eurovision Song Contest Asia was altered in Malaysia.” “We take this matter seriously and will be writing to Voxovation,” Green added. TV3 has yet to comment on the incident. Here, there are also echoes of the European competition: Eurovision has embraced multicultural and pro-LGBTQ+ values to such an extent that countries like Hungary and Turkey have withdrawn due to their governments’ incompatible sociopolitical values. Eurovision Asia’s controversies prove that the European Broadcasting Union has a new – perhaps unexpected – set of geopolitical and sociopolitical values to navigate. Television viewership for Eurovision Asia varied by market. In Vietnam , the show reached over 5 million viewers. The host country’s broadcast , however, only reached an average of 385,000 Thai viewers. These numbers pale in comparison to Eurovision 2026’s viewership of 131 million viewers across the 35 competing nations. Nonetheless, hype is already building for the 2027 edition of Eurovision Asia. During a news conference in Bangkok, Voxovation executive Christer Björkman confirmed that multiple cities have expressed interest in hosting, with China, Japan and Taiwan indicating that they’re open to participating in the future. If more Asian broadcasters buy in, Eurovision will attract an even larger international audience, bringing Voxovation one step closer to turning the contest from a European tradition into a global phenomenon. But time will tell whether Eurovision Asia can become something more than a European competition staged elsewhere. title: Oscar Wilde had a surprising rapport with Colorado miners – why it is hard to imagine that happening today
excerpt: In 1882, Oscar Wilde toured the U.S. lecturing about art and aesthetics. Napoleon Sarony/Wikimedia Commons Oscar Wilde, the Victorian writer of “ The Picture of Dorian Gray ” and “ The Importance of Being Earnest ,” was a fashionable icon known as much for his refined manner and conversation as for his writings. So the image of Wilde exploring Colorado’s frontier towns and rugged mines sounds like a scene from a dream. But that is exactly what happened during his extensive tour of the U.S. in 1882. Wilde arrived in the U.S. from Europe with much aplomb. The impresario Richard D’Oyly Carte , the promoter of the acclaimed operetta duo W.S. Gilbert and Arthur Sullivan , bankrolled Wilde’s tour. Gilbert and Sullivan had recently written a new comic opera, “ Patience ,” which mocked the aesthetic movement , of which Wilde was an icon. Championing artifice and refinement in all aspects of life, aesthetes dressed in ornate, unusual ways, such as Wilde’s habit of wearing an unnatural green carnation on his lapel. The often-mocked figure of the dandy , a wealthy man who dressed in the most bizarre and fanciful fashions of day, was an inspiration for aesthetes. I study 19th-century literature in the English-speaking world , and I see Wilde’s western journey to my home state of Colorado as an example of how intellectual writers in the Victorian era were interested in the working class and how that curiosity was, perhaps surprisingly, mutual. Wilde’s journey to the ‘Wild West’ Carte brought Wilde to America around the time of the U.S. premiere of “Patience” to help popularize the idea of the aesthete. While on tour, Wilde visited major cities, such as New York and Philadelphia, giving almost 100 interviews . But he also was interested in the “Wild West.” His curiosity may seem paradoxical: Tawdry saloons and dusty main streets were a stark contrast to the atmosphere of luxurious refinement he cultivated. Yet, above all, Wilde craved the novel and unexpected. He sought experiences and people who were the opposite of the conventionality he saw as chaining Victorian society. The slightly anarchic roughness of the West appealed to him. He called it “the most beautiful part” of the country. Wilde arrived in Colorado Springs in April 1882 . Railroad baron William Jackson Palmer had founded this booming resort town in 1871 . The town, a short railway journey from Denver, served as a health retreat for those suffering from tuberculosis – one of the deadliest diseases in the nation at the time. Befitting its growing popularity, Colorado Springs had a thriving arts scene. According to the Colorado Springs Pioneers Museum , “interest in the arts began almost immediately” and was distinguished by the opening of an opera house in 1881. Crafting it in red brick and sandstone, the architects took inspiration from Madison Square Theater in New York. It became one of the most impressive buildings in the state. Wilde gave his lecture on “ The Decorative Arts ” at this opera house. He did not condescend to his Colorado audience, nor did he suggest that the highest quality art could only exist in the refined settings of Europe. Instead, he insisted that art should be a part of ordinary existence. “Art,” he declared , “is not something which you can take or leave” but rather “a necessity of human life.” For Wilde, art meant “value to the workman” and “the pleasure which he must necessarily take in making a beautiful thing.” The quality of art for Wilde was not about luxury and extravagance but about creativity and honesty in creation. Oscar Wilde dressed the part of ‘high’ art in the 19th century. ilbusca/iStock via Getty Images Plus The local paper, The Daily Gazette – now The Gazette – reviewed his talk positively in a column from April 15, 1882. The column praises Wilde for how “the entire evening he commanded the closest attention of his audience.” Reportedly, when he “would give expression to a brilliant thought or idea a murmur of applause would pass through the audience.” The article finishes by exclaiming that the lecture “was instructive and interesting and appreciated by all who were present.” A dandy among the miners Wilde’s popularity in the West reveals the oversimplistic nature of the divide between the “highbrow” culture of the literati and the culture of “common” society. His visit to the isolated, high-elevation mountain town of Leadville makes this blending of “high” and “low” culture even more vital. In this hardscrabble town, which owed its existence to the hard labor of miners, workers came to the Tabor Opera House to hear the lavish aesthete. Similar to his speech in Colorado Springs, he discussed how “beautiful and rational designs are necessary in all work.” For Wilde, the roughness of his surroundings were closer to his ideal than the conventionality of Eastern U.S. cities, with their “bad wall-papers horribly designed.” In 1882, Oscar Wilde gave a lecture on art at the Tabor Opera House in Leadville, Colo. Jerrye and Roy Klotz MD CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons The relationship between Wilde and his Leadville audience was symbiotic. The artist found what he desired in the hard-edged mountain town, far from the pomp and conventions of Europe. “The revolver was their book of etiquette,” Wilde wrote of the town , not altogether disapprovingly. He drank with miners, some of whom lowered him into the depths of the Matchless Mine, a riotous atmosphere he found rather exciting. The miners, he wrote in his “ Impressions of America ,” were “very charming and not at all rough.” According to Wilde, these miners likewise found value in his discussions about art. Beyond the ‘highbrow-lowbrow’ divide Newspaper articles about Wilde’s lectures in Colorado do not emphasize the cultural gap between him and his audiences. That dynamic may not have seemed odd – other than the novelty of a foreign celebrity visiting towns in the interior of the country. In addition, 19th-century literary culture may not have conceived of the rigid divide between highbrow literati interests and those of the working class that exists today. The historian Lawrence Levine, in his influential 1990 book “ Highbrow/Lowbrow ,” asserts that supposedly elite pursuits actually had wide appeal in 19th-century American culture. For instance, opera was not associated primarily with multimillionaires in fancy tuxedos and evening gowns, but was also a popular pastime for all ages and social classes. That opera houses even existed in the frontier towns of Colorado demonstrates Levine’s point. Working-class residents of Leadville appreciated the chance to hear Wilde lecture about art as much as he relished the chance to travel to a real mining town and talk with its residents. In my view, economic and cultural divides of today can be bridged so everyone can engage intellectual insights and reflections. Witty, sophisticated authors like Wilde do not simply belong to exclusive elite circles. title: Abbott spent 12 years neglecting Texas air pollution – a new governor can start cleaning it up
excerpt: Texas has many air pollution sources, from oil refineries to coal-fired power plants. Sarah L. Voisin/The Washington Post via Getty Images When air quality monitors in 10 Texas counties showed soot above the new federal health limit in 2024, Gov. Greg Abbott faced a choice. He could direct the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to develop plans to cut air pollution in all 10. Or he could heed the agency’s advice : blame six counties’ pollution mostly on sources beyond Texas, and clean up just four. Abbott chose neither. Weeks after President Donald Trump returned to office in 2025, the governor asked the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to declare the entire state in compliance with the federal standard for fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5. If the EPA agreed, Texas would skirt the need to write a plan to control the deadliest air pollutant . As an atmospheric scientist , I was stunned. I had seen Texas and other states do too little to control air pollution for years. But I hadn’t imagined a governor would override his own regulators to avoid making a plan altogether. Texas air pollution had declined for decades, but during Abbott’s 12 years in office, progress in reducing PM2.5 and ozone smog largely stalled. Now, the election of Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa to succeed Abbott in January 2027 offers a chance to get Texas pollution trending downward again. Hinojosa has a history of supporting efforts to clean up pollution, including a climate plan proposed in 2021 to cut emissions. But progress won’t come easily. Abbott’s appointees still run the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, and Republicans still control the state Senate. A deadly legacy PM2.5 is tiny, with diameters of 2.5 microns or less, so it can be inhaled deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Exposure has been linked to heart attacks, strokes, respiratory problems and many other ailments. Some PM2.5 is emitted directly as particles, such as in diesel exhaust and wildfire smoke. Other particles form in the atmosphere from sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbon gases emitted by power plants, vehicles and other sources. Abbott’s dodge of PM2.5 standards fit a pattern of going easy on polluters. Greg Abbott, right, was Texas attorney general before becoming governor. In that role, he testified against EPA regulations on greenhouse gases in Congressional hearings and fought them in the courts. Brendan Smialowski/Getty Images Houston and Dallas have missed deadline after deadline to meet federal ozone standards. State regulators blame much of the smog on foreign sources . This fall, Abbott persuaded the Trump administration to reconsider how severely the two regions’ smog is classified, a step that could loosen the pollution controls required there. Under Abbott, state regulators have also rarely cracked down on unauthorized pollution releases. Of 21,769 such events reported by refineries, chemical plants and other facilities over six years, they classified fewer than 1% as “excessive,” the designation that requires a company to fix the problem. The fight over scrubbers Texas’ coal power plants emit more sulfur dioxide than any other state’s. That gas forms sulfate particles, a major ingredient of PM2.5 and haze. Federal rules have required new coal plants to install scrubbers, which remove sulfur dioxide from smokestack gases, since 1979. But older plants were exempted, and several in Texas still run without them. A 2016 Obama administration plan to reduce Texas’ haze and a narrower Biden administration proposal in 2023 would have required several plants to install or upgrade scrubbers. In 2025 the Trump administration accepted Texas’ own haze plans , which required no new scrubbers. Critics of the federal plans had warned that some plants would close instead because of the cost, reducing electricity supplies. But scrubbers are a long-established technology, and their health benefits dwarf their costs . When I worked at Georgia’s environmental agency in the mid-2000s, we negotiated a timetable for Georgia Power to install scrubbers and retire outdated plants. Atlanta’s PM2.5 levels fell about 40% over the next decade, and the lights stayed on just fine. The W.A. Parish Electric Generating Station in Fort Bend County, Texas, is a major source of air pollution. Three of its four coal units have no scrubbers. RM VM via Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA Research by my group at Rice University has found that PM2.5 from Texas coal plants, formed mostly from their sulfur dioxide, kills hundreds of people a year. Wind and solar power or geothermal energy could replace their output, with batteries filling in when winds are slow and sunshine weak. No polluter has benefited more from Abbott’s neglect than the W.A. Parish power plant, whose smokestacks loom over my hikes at Brazos Bend State Park southwest of Houston. Three of its four coal units have no scrubbers at all . Parish emitted three times as much sulfur dioxide as all other facilities in the Houston region combined in 2024. Our modeling linked its pollution to 177 deaths a year. Since sulfate, which forms from sulfur dioxide, is the second-largest ingredient in Houston’s PM2.5 , any serious cleanup plan would have to tackle Parish. Clearing the air Hinojosa’s first test will come within weeks of her inauguration, when the U.S. EPA faces a court-ordered deadline to announce which counties violate its PM2.5 standard. The number of Texas counties exceeding the limit is now at 14 . Wildfire smoke and other exceptional events may explain some of the problem, but most of those counties need plans to cut the local emissions driving their PM2.5 levels. Gina Hinojosa, a Democrat, was elected in November 2026 to be Texas’ next governor. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Hinojosa can withdraw Abbott’s zero-county request and ask the EPA to designate counties as failing to meet the standard where the data warrants it, triggering a need to write cleanup plans. In my view, those plans should start with overdue controls on emissions at the dirtiest coal plants. The state also needs to cut pollution from refineries, chemical plants, industrial flares and ports to meet the standards. Expanding grants to replace old diesel engines would cut soot and smog. Better plans would include more monitors. Many counties, including Fort Bend, Texas’ eighth-most-populous county and home to Parish, don’t have a single PM2.5 monitor . Others don’t measure what their PM2.5 is made of. Because PM2.5 is a stew of carbon, sulfate, nitrate, ammonium, dust and other compounds, knowing the mix is key to controlling it cost-effectively. Abbott spent 12 years explaining away Texas’ dirty air. A new governor can finally clear it. title: Lowering fuel-efficiency standards for cars could cost Americans more, not save them money
excerpt: Buying more gas is a direct consequence of driving a less fuel-efficient vehicle. Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images When looking to purchase a car, many people hesitate to buy one that could reduce their fuel costs, even when gas prices are high. The Trump administration has made that decision more complex for consumers. Cars with lower fuel costs tend to be more expensive to purchase , may be inconvenient to refuel or may have less trunk space . Conventional gasoline engine models often have lower up-front prices and standard features, including easy refueling and cargo space, which keeps consumers buying them. Since taking office, the Trump administration has eliminated limits on greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles and rolled back future standards for vehicle fuel efficiency , allowing future passenger vehicles to consume more gas per mile traveled than what would have been allowed under existing rules. The administration claimed those actions would save people money . Specifically, the administration said the fact that it’s cheaper to build less-efficient cars would mean consumers would pay prices so low that the savings would offset any additional costs for fuel over the life of the car. However, the article we recently published in the journal Science explains that the administration’s decision is based on several flawed assumptions , including how much buyers care about their cars’ future fuel costs. We found that the administration’s regulation changes will leave U.S. car buyers worse off because they will spend far more on gas relative to the up-front price savings, especially if gasoline prices remain high for a long period. An example of fuel efficiency savings Take a look at two comparable cars : a gas-powered 2026 Toyota Corolla and a 2026 Toyota Corolla hybrid powered with a combination of gas and electricity. The base model hybrid costs $1,800 more to buy than the base model gas-powered car. The gas car has an average fuel efficiency of 34 miles per gallon; the hybrid’s is 50 miles per gallon. To drive the same distance, the hybrid’s increased efficiency saves $550 a year in fuel costs, assuming gas costs $4 per gallon . So after about three years and a few months, the gas savings of the Toyota hybrid will have evened out its higher purchase price. Some cars take longer to break even: The fuel savings from a Honda Accord hybrid will take about eight years. But the average car is nearly 13 years old – meaning fuel savings will continue for a decade after the owner has broken even on the higher sticker price. Examining economic assumptions In its analysis of the economic effects of the loosened restrictions, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency assumed that consumers sacrifice valuable vehicle features when buying a more fuel-efficient vehicle. For instance, the agency pointed to people being annoyed by certain fuel-saving technologies such as stop-start ignition , which shuts off the engine at a red light in certain types of vehicles, or the difficulty of charging an electric vehicle away from home . It projected that people prefer cars without stop-start ignition and without the need to charge batteries. Furthermore, the EPA assumed that gasoline prices would never exceed $3.50 per gallon , a level far lower than current average prices. While the EPA agreed that a less-fuel-efficient car would cost more to refuel, it also claimed that consumers would lose about 75% to 79% of those fuel cost savings because of unhappiness with certain fuel-saving technologies or the inconvenience of refueling electric vehicles. However, after reviewing studies on how much people value different attributes of various vehicles, we found the evidence showed consumers would be willing to pay only 17% to 31% of those additional fuel costs. Therefore, while consumers would pay a lower up-front purchase price if fuel-efficiency standards remained high, they would not find enough value in desirable features on the cars to make up for higher recurring spending on gasoline. And that does not even consider the environmental costs, including damage associated with greenhouse gas emissions, which is influencing U.S. car buyers’ choices . In fact, given the recent improvement in features of EVs and charging infrastructure, we believe that the agencies may have overestimated those costs by even more. Many current new EVs have around 300 miles of range before needing to be recharged. That’s much farther than cars available even five years ago. In late 2025, Ford stopped building its F-150 Lightning all-electric truck. Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images Messages to car manufacturers Making matters more difficult for consumers is the fact that recent presidents have sent mixed messages to automakers. The Obama administration set aggressive standards for improving fuel economy and reducing greenhouse gas emissions . The first Trump administration rolled back those standards . The Biden administration not only reinstated the Obama standards but went beyond them , requiring further increases in fuel efficiency and emissions reductions. President Donald Trump is joined by Cabinet members, lawmakers and car company executives in December 2025 to announce the weakening of fuel efficiency standards. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images The second Trump administration’s moves to reverse the Biden standards have left automakers unclear about how to develop long-term plans for what to build and sell. That planning happens years in advance . In 2025, when Trump discontinued federal tax subsidies to help people buy electric cars, automakers stopped building as many . With the fuel-efficiency changes, many automakers have shifted away from introducing new EV models and toward promoting gasoline models . Fewer electric cars makes it more challenging for people to buy them . In the U.S., according to September 2026 sales data, all-electric cars account for about 7% of new car sales – while in China, where electric cars abound and are subsidized by the government, around 40% of new cars people bought in 2026 were all-electric. Our work finds that eliminating the greenhouse gas emissions standards and weakening the fuel-efficiency rules will bring Americans more pain at the pump and hurt people’s wallets, making living less affordable. title: Independent, Gen Z and Latino voters helped deliver a Democratic wave in 2026 – but that doesn’t mean a lasting realignment
excerpt: Attendees await the arrival of Democratic candidates Gina Hinojosa for Texas governor, James Talarico for the U.S. Senate and Bobby Pulido for the U.S. House at a rally on Oct. 25, 2026, in Weslaco, Texas. AP Photo/Michael Gonzalez The Democratic wave in the 2026 midterm elections raises an important question about American politics. Are independent, Gen Z and Latino voters building a new Democratic coalition, or are they sending a warning to both parties that their support cannot be taken for granted? The preliminary evidence suggests something more complicated. Our analysis, including a deep dive into the 2026 Voter Poll conducted by the market research firm SSRS , points to three factors behind the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories: a substantial shift among independent voters toward Democratic candidates, stronger Democratic turnout relative to Republicans, and declining enthusiasm among voters who supported Donald Trump in 2024. Gen Z, who are people born from 1997 to 2012, and Latino voters played important roles in these shifts. But the results should not automatically be interpreted as a lasting Democratic realignment. These voters may be demonstrating a willingness to reconsider their political choices when governing parties fail to meet their expectations. The overlapping influence of independent, younger and Latino voters helps explain the scale of the Democratic gains. Our analysis, based on voter poll data , suggests that independents, who made up about one-third of voters, contributed approximately 52% of the Democrats’ national popular vote margin in House races. Latino voters contributed an estimated 23% of that margin, while voters ages 18 to 29 contributed approximately 39%. Because these groups overlap, their contributions cannot be added together. But the figures illustrate how important each was to the Democratic advantage. In our book, “ The Independent Voter ,” co-authored with Omar Ali, we examine the growing influence of independent voters and their often unpredictable voting behavior. Independents helped determine the outcome Independent voters, among the most important contributors to Democratic victories in the 2026 midterms, have repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to shift between parties. In 2008, they favored Democratic presidential candidate Barack Obama by 8 percentage points. Four years later, they backed Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney by 5 points. In the 2016 presidential election, independents favored Republican Trump by 4 points before swinging toward Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 , supporting him by 13 points. In the 2024 presidential election, independents narrowly favored Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump, 49% to 46%. However, Trump performed better among independents in key battleground states, including Arizona , Georgia , Pennsylvania and North Carolina . In our research spanning nearly five decades , Dan Hunting and I, Thom Reilly, found that independents exhibit considerably greater volatility in their voting patterns than Democrats and Republicans. The 3-point advantage independents gave Harris in 2024 provides a useful baseline for understanding their much larger shift toward Democratic candidates in 2026. A November 2026 national survey of more than 90,000 people found that voters identifying with neither major party favored Democratic House candidates by more than 20 percentage points. Supporters of Alaska independent congressional candidate Bill Hill rally on Nov. 3, 2026, in Anchorage. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Our analysis of voter poll data showed that independents favored House Democrats by 59% to 37%. In addition, independents’ support was consequential in several Republican-held Senate seats that flipped to Democrats, with independent voters providing the margin needed for victory in six of the nine races: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi, Ohio and South Carolina. The emerging pattern may represent another turn in a longer cycle of electoral volatility among independents. Rather than embracing either party, independent voters appear willing to reconsider their choices as political and economic conditions change. Did Republicans switch sides or stay home? There is some disagreement about what produced the midterm Democratic wave. Brookings scholars Elaine Kamarck and William Galston argue that Republican abstention – those who chose not to vote – was more important nationally than large-scale partisan crossover voting. They report that only approximately 6% of self-identified Republicans voted for Democratic House candidates. Yet the evidence also demonstrates some crossover voting. An analysis by the research firm NORC found that approximately 1 in 10 2024 Trump voters in 2026 supported Democratic Senate candidates in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina and Texas. Both dynamics appear to have played a role. Democrats benefited from stronger participation among their supporters and reduced turnout among some voters who backed Trump in 2024. In several competitive races, Republican defections and strong independent support also contributed to Democratic victories. Understanding these differences is important. A shift in election results does not necessarily mean voters have changed their party loyalties. It may reflect changes in who participates. The 2026 results suggest that both factors were at work. Younger voters shifted sharply toward Democrats Gen Z voters were another important part of the Democratic gains. In 2026, 66% of voters ages 18–29 supported Democratic House candidates, compared with 30% who backed Republicans. That 36-point Democratic advantage was substantially larger than the 14-point margin in 2024, according to Tufts University . There was also evidence of voters switching party choices. Among young people who voted for Trump in 2024 and participated in the 2026 election, 16% supported a Democratic House candidate. And 67% of young voters disapproved of Trump’s performance as president in 2026. Gallup found that 56% of Gen Z adults identify as political independents, underscoring the weaker ties many younger Americans have to the two major parties. Combined with economic dissatisfaction and distrust of political institutions , this suggests that younger voters may be especially willing to reconsider their choices when the party in power fails to meet their expectations or deliver on its promises. Latino voters also shifted substantially Latino voters showed a similar pattern, but with some differences. More than 6 in 10 Latino voters supported Democratic House candidates in 2026, according to a NORC survey . That reverses much of the Republican gains among these voters in 2024. There was also evidence of volatility among Latinos. A postelection survey by UnidosUS and BSP Research found that 17% of Latino voters who supported Trump in 2024 voted for Democratic House candidates in 2026, compared with just 3% of Harris voters who supported Republicans. Texas offers an example of how these voting groups overlapped. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, candidate for U.S. House Bobby Pulido and U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico pose for photos at a campaign rally on Oct. 25, 2026, in Weslaco, Texas. Brandon Bell/Getty Images According to our analysis of the voter poll data , 68% of Latino voters supported Democrat James Talarico, compared with 30% who backed his Republican opponent. Among voters ages 18 to 29, Talarico won 79% to 19%, while independents favored him by 64% to 33%. Of course, these groups overlap. A voter can be Latino, young and independent, so their contributions cannot simply be added together numerically. Still, Latinos’ strong support for Talarico illustrates how shifts among these voting groups helped Democrats win in a traditionally Republican state, perhaps shaping a new composite demographic. A warning for both political parties The lesson of 2026 may be less about Democratic realignment than about political accountability. Republicans benefited in 2024 from dissatisfaction with Democratic governance. Two years later, Democrats benefited from dissatisfaction with Republican governance. Yet the scale of the Democratic victories should not be understated. Widespread dissatisfaction with Trump’s presidency – his handling of the economy, the war in Iran, harsh immigration enforcement policies and concerns about corruption – contributed to a sweeping rejection of his administration and Republican leadership at both the federal and state levels. That includes a Congress that many voters believed had failed to hold him accountable. Even so, neither party should assume that independents, younger voters or Latinos now belong to its camp. America’s founders recognized the dangers of excessive party loyalty . In his 1796 farewell address , George Washington warned about the divisive influence of political parties and the dangers of placing party allegiance above the public interest. More than two centuries later, the growing influence of voters with weaker ties to the major parties raises a similar question about the role of political parties in American democracy. The 2026 election may not signal a lasting political realignment. Instead, it may reflect an electorate increasingly willing to hold both parties accountable. For Democrats and Republicans alike, winning an election does not necessarily mean winning voters’ lasting loyalty. title: What is ‘intergenerational trauma’? A social worker explains how one generation’s experiences can affect descendants
excerpt: Consequences of traumatic experiences, such as becoming a refugee, can reverberate across future generations. linephoto/iStock via Getty Images Plus Throughout history, millions of people have experienced widespread violence, persecution and loss. During the Holocaust, 6 million Jewish people were murdered . Beginning in 1619 and through the mid-1800s, 12.5 million African people were forced onto ships during the trans-Atlantic slave trade . These are just two examples of many that have affected communities in ways that last long after the initial experiences. Such traumas can have lasting consequences for a person’s physical and mental health . Yet, these effects may extend beyond those directly affected. Some can change the psychological, emotional and social well-being of a person’s children and grandchildren. This phenomenon, known as “intergenerational trauma,” describes how the effects of trauma can extend across generations. This can occur even when descendants have not experienced the original events . Intergenerational trauma can come from individual experiences, such as childhood abuse or family violence. But researchers have primarily studied it in relation to collective experiences . These can include genocide, enslavement, colonization, war or forced displacement – when unrest or famine force people to leave their homes. I am a professor of social work . My research with immigrants and refugees looks at how collective and historical traumas shape individual and community well-being across generations. My work also explores how culture helps people cope with hardship, heal and recover together as groups. How trauma crosses generations Intergenerational trauma gained wider attention in the 1990s . Studies of Holocaust survivors and their children helped bring the issue to light. Researchers in the United States, Europe and Israel studied families affected by persecution, displacement and profound loss. They explored how these events shaped the mental health of descendants who had never lived through them . Over time, scholars have found multiple relational paths through which the consequences of trauma can extend across generations . For example, fear can shape parenting , and a parent’s silence can make their distress hard to understand. Trauma can also weaken community ties. Biological changes may also occur through what’s called epigenetics. These changes can affect how cells use genes while leaving the DNA code intact. This may also help explain how the effects of trauma reach later generations. A study of three generations of Syrian refugee families, for instance, found a link between exposure to wartime violence and chemical marks on DNA . Scientists still don’t know whether parents can pass these marks to their children or if they affect how their children respond to stress. Lasting effects of collective and historical trauma Recognizing intergenerational trauma helps trace how experiences affect entire communities , not just individuals. Closely related is the concept of “historical trauma” or “collective trauma.” These describe the cumulative effects of collective experiences , not just one-time events, over time. Examples are colonization, genocide and ongoing discrimination and mistreatment across generations. For example, researchers have studied how colonization and family separation continue to affect the mental, social and physical health of generations of Indigenous peoples. They have looked at the lasting effects of government policies that forced Indigenous people to adopt the dominant culture . These policies barred people from speaking their own languages and practicing their traditions . More than 200,000 Indigenous children were forced into residential schools in the U.S. and Canada in the 19th and 20th centuries. In Canada, for instance, First Nations, Inuit and Métis children were forcibly sent to residential schools between 1831 and 1997. Studies have linked their attendance to psychological distress among descendants . Likewise, in the U.S. in the 19th and 20th centuries, the federal government operated or supported Native American boarding schools . Research shows a link between fathers’ attendance and chronic health problems in their adult children . In Australia, researchers have found higher rates of mental health problems among descendants of the “Stolen Generations.” These were Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children forcibly removed from their families from the mid-1800s into the 1970s . Among Black Americans, scholars have shown how the historical legacies of enslavement and racial violence intersect with current experiences of racism . These collective experiences may shape family narratives, cultural identity and psychological well-being across generations. Many immigrant and refugee communities also experience historical trauma. A review of studies on collective trauma among forced migrants displaced by war, persecution or political violence shows they often navigate the effects of loss and separation long after they move to a new country . Research has identified parental distress, cultural identity and changing family roles as ways these experiences affect descendants . Similarly, colleagues and I examined previous research that also highlights how these effects can shape the lives of subsequent generations of migrant families . Across these populations, intergenerational trauma involves more than the passing on of psychological distress within families . When subsequent generations experience discrimination or continued threats to their cultural identity, the consequences of past trauma can intersect with new hardships . Cultural practices in communities that have experienced colonization can support resilience. chameleonseye/iStock via Getty Images Plus From intergenerational trauma to intergenerational resilience Just as the consequences of trauma can extend beyond the generation that experienced it, so can resilience. In my work with immigrants and refugees, I have found that intergenerational trauma is neither inevitable nor uniform across communities. Psychological outcomes vary among descendants of trauma survivors. For instance, in one study of adult children of Holocaust survivors, about 1 in 3 had experienced post-traumatic stress disorder if both parents had it. Fewer than 1 in 10 had experienced PTSD if neither parent had it. Families and communities pass down cultural traditions, stories of survival, collective healing and shared identities too. These can help future generations navigate adversity . An intergenerational trauma perspective recognizes that healing involves families and communities. It may mean addressing pain within groups and offering mental health care that respects culture. These can be community-based approaches that create opportunities for shared understanding, connection and healing. Individuals and communities do not need to be defined by the suffering of their ancestors. Rather, the concept of intergenerational traumas helps recognize how past experiences can continue to shape the present. It also acknowledges that these influences do not determine the future. The experiences of previous generations can leave lasting wounds. But they can also provide foundations for strength, connection and healing. title: Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes therapies show great promise – but treatment is only effective if people can access it
excerpt: The number of people living with diabetes across the world is climbing. andreswd/E+ via Getty Images In 2026, over 830 million people worldwide are estimated to live with diabetes – more than ever before. Most live in low- and middle-income countries, and over 90% live with Type 2 diabetes , a condition where the body cannot use insulin properly. The second most common form of diabetes is Type 1 , caused by the immune system attacking insulin-producing cells. A 2023 analysis used existing data to model the future burden of diabetes. It estimates that by 2050, more than 1.3 billion people will have diabetes . In North Africa and the Middle East, nearly 17% of people may be affected. In Latin America and the Caribbean, that number could be 11%. Diabetes increases risks of dying early as well as developing a range of complications, including eye, kidney and heart disease. It also affects mental health and well-being . Despite these climbing numbers, there are plenty of reasons to be hopeful about the future of diabetes. I like to regularly remind myself of them, as a healthcare researcher who has lived with Type 1 diabetes for over 30 years. New treatments are on the horizon, and high-profile people with diabetes are speaking about the condition, raising awareness of the need for better treatments and access to care. In September, Alexander Zerev won the U.S. Open tennis championship ; in October, Garret Mitchell won the baseball World Series ; and in November, James Talarico was elected to the U.S. Senate. Talarico has used his experience to advocate for lower insulin costs , as has New Hampshire representative-elect Stefany Shaneen, whose daughter lives with Type 1 . James Talarico, newly elected to the U.S. Senate, talks openly about living with diabetes and uses his experience to advocate for lower insulin costs. Mark Makela/Getty Images The search for a cure for Type 1 diabetes There is no one single cause of either type of diabetes . Genetics, age, race, ethnicity, weight, smoking, diet and physical activity can all contribute to the development of Type 2. Type 1 is thought to be caused by genetics and the environment. Without being able to pinpoint one specific cause, cures have largely proved elusive. When I was diagnosed in the early 1990s, I was told that a cure for Type 1 would be on its way in the next few years. Some 30 years later, a cure that works for most people has yet to arrive. But promising results are coming out for treatments in which insulin-producing cells are either grown in a lab or taken from people who have died and then transplanted into people with Type 1. In clinical trials, the majority of people receiving transplanted insulin-producing cells either no longer needed insulin or could take significantly lower doses . Reducing the amount of insulin they needed reduced their chance of developing severely low blood sugar levels, which can be fatal. The challenge, though, is the risk the body will recognize the new cells as foreign and launch an immune response against them . For people with Type 1, the risk is even greater because their body has already attacked its own insulin-producing cells , meaning their immune systems already see insulin-producing cells as foreign. Medications can help, but for most people, the risks of a lifetime on immunosuppressants outweigh the benefits of living without Type 1 diabetes. Other new and exciting developments are afoot, though. These include changing the cells before they are implanted so the immune system won’t attack them in the first place, as well as using targeted medications that would stop the immune system from attacking insulin-producing cells without making someone immunocompromised – in other words, leaving the rest of the immune system intact. Catching it early Treatments that delay progression of type 1 diabetes – rather than just treating its symptoms – are already available. In the past few years, research has shown that the drug teplizumab can delay the progression of Type 1 diabetes by slowing down the destruction of insulin-producing cells in people whose immune systems have started to attack them. This can delay the need to start insulin for up to three years. Those three years allow people and their families time to plan. And they give children time to mature and live life without insulin injections, blood sugar checks and all the disruption that diabetes can bring. While a healthy diet and exercise are key factors in preventing and managing diabetes, medications are essential for many people. We Are/DigitalVision via Getty Images Screening options Type 1 diabetes has no known single cause , but you’re more likely to get it if a close family member has it. In the U.S., people who don’t yet have symptoms can be screened for early Type 1 if a family member lives with the disease. A blood test can identify the body’s attack on insulin-producing cells far before any symptoms show up, and before blood sugars start rising. If you’re at risk of Type 1 because a family member lives with it, you can either take a sample of your blood at home and send it to a lab, or have the sample drawn at a doctor’s office. It is then sent away for special testing to see if the blood contains markers that show the immune system is targeting insulin-producing cells. This allows people to get early treatment with drugs that can slow the progression of Type 1 diabetes. My kids received a blood test at their doctor’s office through a program called TrialNet , a long-running research partnership that operates across North America, Europe and Australia. We received the results within weeks and found that neither of them had early signs of Type 1 diabetes at the time. We will retest every few years – though they don’t have signs now, their immune systems could start targeting their insulin-producing cells in the future. Because 90% people diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes don’t have a family member who lives with it , European experts are calling to roll out screening for everyone , not just those at heightened risk. More effective treatment programs for Type 2 diabetes Science also offers reasons to be hopeful when it comes to Type 2 diabetes. A clinical trial published in October 2026, involving nearly 100 people with early-onset Type 2, found that over half of participants saw their diabetes go into remission six months after starting a low-calorie diet and supervised exercise program. Similarly, a 2025 study showed that an AI-driven mobile application providing personalized lifestyle advice for diet, physical activity and sleep led to sustained remission in over half of participants for up to three years. New studies are also showing that GLP-1 medications not only lower blood sugar, but they also reduce deaths, hospitalizations and amputations in high-risk populations with Type 2 diabetes. Other recent studies have shown that GLP-1s can prevent the onset of Type 2 in people with elevated blood sugar levels. Unequal access to treatment However, these causes for hope only lead to meaningful change when healthcare is available. Because of lack of access to testing , researchers estimate that more than 250 million people worldwide are unaware that they live with Type 2 diabetes . This means that they can’t make efforts to reverse or treat it. Only about 1 in 2 people across the globe with Type 2 diabetes have access to the insulin they need. GLP-1 access is concentrated in high-income countries , and costs can be prohibitive . Similarly, screening and early treatment for Type 1 diabetes are rarely available across low- and middle-income countries . There is no doubt that if and when a cure comes, many will not be able to access it. My team’s research found that the COVID-19 pandemic made it even more difficult for people to access diabetes care. A nonprofit group I work with called T1International regularly surveys people living with diabetes about their ability to access their essential supplies. In its latest survey, more than a third of the over 1,000 participants had rationed their diabetes supplies in the past year because of cost. But here again, research offers hope. Scientists are looking for ways to make insulin easier to manufacture and distribute. Growing attention on improving access to insulin and diabetes care could provide a powerful catalyst for change. In 1923, Frederick Banting, the Canadian scientist who co-discovered insulin , famously sold its patent for one Canadian dollar, saying “ Insulin is not for me, it is for the world .” Much still needs to be done to achieve that vision – not only for insulin, but for the new scientific discoveries in the pipeline. Jamie Hartmann-Boyce has received diabetes-related research funding from the World Health Organization, the British Heart Foundation, and the University of Oxford. She is a research fellow (unpaid) with T1International.

title: Nonprofit Common Space will launch 1st 'humanitarian satellite' in 2027
excerpt: The first satellite in a constellation designed for humanitarian use will lift off next year, if all goes according to plan. The nonprofit Common Space plans to assemble a six-spacecraft constellation of Earth-observing satellites , whose high-resolution imagery will aid first responders, journalists, scientists and human-rights investigators around the world.
